title: Lower cardinality estimate for substring-match table filters
hypothesis: Every non-equality table filter is costed with a flat DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY=0.2 (relation_statistics_helper.cpp:146-151; same constant in relation_manager.cpp:199/258/276/293/374 for filters left in a LogicalFilter). A predicate that requires a literal substring (contains(col,'lit'), col LIKE '%lit%', LIKE '%a%b%') is usually far more selective than a range comparison. Evidence from q09: p_name LIKE '%ghost%' is actually about 5% selective. EXPLAIN estimates 1,256,266 rows for lineitem⋈part⋈orders and 5,057,324 for the top join, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 324,507 rows, a 4-15x overestimate. Because of that the optimizer builds hash tables on orders (1.5M rows) and on partsupp⋈supplier⋈nation (800k rows), and each of those two joins costs about 0.22-0.23s CPU, while the real probe side is only 324k rows. With a better estimate the join order and build sides can put the small filtered side on the build side.
plan: In RelationStatisticsHelper::ExtractGetStats (src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, around lines 119-155), when no equality filter fired, check whether any non-optional table filter is an ExpressionFilter whose expression is a positive substring-containment test: a BoundFunctionExpression named 'contains', or '~~' / 'like_escape' whose constant pattern starts with '%' and contains at least one non-wildcard character, possibly nested under CONJUNCTION_AND. Do not match negations (!~~, NOT). If one is found, use base_cardinality * SUBSTRING_MATCH_SELECTIVITY, defined as DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY*DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY (0.04) in relation_statistics_helper.hpp, instead of 0.2. Apply the same classification in relation_manager.cpp where a LogicalFilter's expressions fall back to DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY: add a small static helper IsSubstringMatchPredicate(const Expression&) to RelationStatisticsHelper and reuse it in both places. Before and after the change, check with EXPLAIN on q09/q16 that the estimates move and that the join order changes. Run the full visible bench, since plans may change elsewhere.
expected_gain: q09 (18% of total): possibly 20-40% if the orders/partsupp builds shrink or the join order changes. Smaller effects possible on q16 (s_comment LIKE '%..%..%' under NOT IN) and on other templates with LIKE '%x%' on a dimension table. Roughly 3-8% on the visible geomean if q09 moves.
generality: Any star or snowflake join where a dimension is filtered by a substring/contains predicate (text search on names or comments) now gets a realistic, smaller cardinality, so it is placed on the build side and joined early. Possible regressions: substring predicates that are actually unselective (for example '%a%') will be underestimated, which could put a big relation on the build side. That risk is bounded because the build-side flip and the hash join still work correctly, only slower.
risk: Medium. The change only affects cost estimates, so results stay correct, but plans for other templates may change, possibly for the worse. The selectivity constant is a heuristic derived from DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY, not tuned to the data. If the bench shows a mixed result, try applying it only when the literal has at least 3 characters before giving up.

title: Investigate high-cardinality hash aggregation cost after outer join
hypothesis: In q13, HASH_GROUP_BY on a single integer key (c_custkey) over 1.53M rows into 150k groups costs 0.20s CPU, about 130ns/row and the largest operator in the 2nd slowest template. The group key comes from the build side of a RIGHT join and has tight min/max stats [1,150000]. Each of the 8 threads sees nearly every group (reduction only about 1.3x per thread), so the thread-local tables give little benefit before repartitioning. DecideAdaptation in radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:424 skips lookups only when the HLL unique share is above 0.95.
plan: First profile only (perf on q13), to see whether the cost is in the local sink, the repartition, or the finalize/combine. Candidate fixes, to be chosen after profiling: (a) when the estimated group count from stats is close to the row count per thread, start in skip-lookup/partition-only mode earlier; (b) a dense-range direct aggregation path for a single integer key with a small stats range and simple aggregates. Do not change the perfect_ht_threshold default, which is a setting.
expected_gain: q13 maybe 20-30%. Any template with a GROUP BY on a high-cardinality key (q18 subquery GROUP BY l_orderkey) may also benefit.
generality: GROUP BY on a high-cardinality key with low per-thread reduction, a common pattern in analytical queries (per-customer or per-order aggregates).
risk: Medium-high. The aggregate hash table is heavily tuned, so a constant tweak can regress low-cardinality aggregates. It needs a profile before any coding.

title: Substring-match scan selectivity (minimal, finish E0001)
hypothesis: q09 (123.8ms, slowest template) builds hash joins on orders (1.5M) and partsupp (800k) while the real probe side is about 324k rows. The cause is that the part scan filter contains(p_name,'ghost'), pushed down from LIKE '%ghost%', is estimated at DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY 0.2 (about 40k rows), but only about 5% of rows pass. EXPLAIN shows estimates of about 1.26M rows for lineitem⋈part⋈orders and 5.06M for the top join. E0001 did not fail as an idea: the implementer ran out of time while building, and it was never benchmarked. If the part estimate drops to about 8k, the join-order optimizer should make the filtered part/lineitem side the build side.
plan: Keep the diff small and out of the header, so the rebuild stays short. In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, add a file-local static helper IsSubstringMatchFilter(const TableFilter&). It returns true for an ExpressionFilter whose expression is contains(col, non-empty VARCHAR constant), or ~~/like_escape with a constant pattern that starts with '%' and contains a literal character. It recurses into ConjunctionAndFilter children. It never matches OR, NOT or !~~. In ExtractGetStats (around lines 146-151), when no equality filter applied and some non-optional table filter matches, use selectivity 0.04 (a file-local constexpr) instead of DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY. Leave relation_manager.cpp unchanged in this experiment. Then: build in the background, EXPLAIN q09.m0 and confirm the part estimate falls to about 8k and the join order changes, then run the full bench.
expected_gain: q09: 20-40% if the build sides flip. Other templates with LIKE '%x%' filters on a dimension table (q13-like, q16, q14 variants) may change their plans. Geomean: 1-3%.
generality: Any query with a substring LIKE or contains filter on a table that is joined. Substring filters are usually much more selective than 0.2. A query whose substring filter matches most rows could get a worse join order, since the estimate would be about 5x too low.
risk: Low-medium. Only estimates change, so results stay correct. Plan changes on hidden templates could regress some. Mitigation if results are mixed: apply the lower selectivity only when the literal is at least 3 characters.

title: Cardinality-aware perfect hash aggregation above the bit threshold
hypothesis: q13 (the second-slowest template, about 97ms) spends 0.20s CPU in HASH_GROUP_BY on a single integer key (c_custkey, stats [1,150000], 18 bits) over 1.53M rows into 150k groups. The radix hash table gets little benefit from thread-local pre-aggregation here, because each thread sees most of the groups. CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (src/execution/physical_plan/plan_aggregate.cpp:127) refuses perfect hashing because 18 bits is more than perfect_ht_threshold (12). I measured this directly with `SET perfect_ht_threshold=20`: the plan becomes PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY at 0.04s CPU, and the hot wall time of the q13 inner query falls from about 107ms to about 73ms (-30%). Counter-evidence that makes a guard necessary: the q18-style `GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>300` over lineitem (23 bits, 1.5M groups, 6M rows) goes from 76ms to 800-1040ms with threshold 24. Each thread allocates and initialises a 2^bits table, and the global Combine and the scan are O(2^bits) and serial. So perfect hashing pays off only when the dense table is small compared with the input.
plan: In plan_aggregate.cpp only, with no header changes and the setting's default unchanged: keep the existing check (perfect_hash_bits <= perfect_ht_threshold, which accepts as today). When that check fails, accept anyway if all of the following hold: (1) perfect_hash_bits <= a file-local constexpr cap of 20 bits (1M slots); (2) the aggregate child's estimated_cardinality is known and (1 << perfect_hash_bits) * number_of_threads <= 2 * estimated_cardinality (the per-thread tables are no larger than about twice the input, so allocation, initialisation and combine stay proportional to the input); (3) every other existing condition holds (no grouping sets, no DISTINCT, combine callback present). CanUsePerfectHashAggregate needs the estimate passed in from CreatePlan(LogicalAggregate&) via op.children[0]->estimated_cardinality, and the thread count from TaskScheduler::GetScheduler(context).NumberOfThreads(). If the user set perfect_ht_threshold above the default, the existing check already covers it. Steps: build in the background; EXPLAIN q13.m0 and confirm PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY; EXPLAIN q18.m0 and confirm its large GROUP BY stays HASH_GROUP_BY; then run the full bench. If q13 improves but the estimate is too far off in other cases, tighten the factor of 2 to 1.
expected_gain: q13 about 25-30% (about 97ms → about 70ms), roughly a 2% geomean gain from one template. Any template with GROUP BY on a 13-20 bit dense integer key over many more rows (q18-style per-key aggregates with smaller key ranges, per-customer or per-supplier aggregates) also benefits.
generality: GROUP BY on one or more integer keys with min/max stats whose dense range (2^13 to 2^20) is small compared with the input row count: per-entity aggregates over fact tables after joins to dimension keys. Queries whose estimates are badly wrong (estimate high, actual input small) could get slower from allocating 1M-slot tables per thread. The cap of 20 bits bounds that cost to a few MB per thread.
risk: Low-medium. The diff is one file and planner-only, and it reuses an existing, tested operator, so the risk to correctness is low. The performance risk comes from overestimated cardinality; measured, a 23-bit case was 10x slower, which is why the hard cap and the guard on the ratio to input size exist. The reviewer may ask whether this circumvents the setting. The argument is that the setting is still honoured as the unconditional threshold, and the new rule only adds a cost-based acceptance.

title: Lazy-initialised perfect hash aggregate table with a bounded bit extension
hypothesis: E0003 showed that perfect hashing q13's inner aggregate (18 bits, 1.53M rows, 150k groups) saves about 25% wall time (115->90ms, agg CPU 0.20s->0.04s). It also showed that estimate-based acceptance fails: q13 is underestimated 5x and q17 overestimated 1000x. q17 regressed because PerfectAggregateHashTable's constructor (perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp:28-48) eagerly calls InitializeStates on all 2^bits slots in every thread, and Combine (:163) and Destroy (:289) walk all 2^bits slots. If states are initialised only on first touch, a perfect table on a near-empty input costs one uninitialised malloc and a memset of 2^bits bool flags, so a cardinality-independent bit cap becomes safe for small inputs.
plan: 1) perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp constructor: keep the uninitialised data allocation and the group_is_set memset, and remove the InitializeStates loop. 2) AddChunk (:132-142): when group_is_set[group] is false, set it to true and append the slot address to a new-groups address vector, then call RowOperations::InitializeStates once for those new slots before UpdateStates. Flag first, so a duplicate in the same chunk is not initialised twice. 3) Combine: when the target slot is not set, InitializeStates the target first (batch new targets the same way), then CombineStates. Add a touched-groups counter as a member in perfect_aggregate_hashtable.hpp, incremented on first touch. If other.touched == 0, return early (still move the allocator). Otherwise scan group_is_set 8 bytes at a time (memcpy into uint64_t and skip zero words). 4) Destroy: call destructors only on slots with group_is_set (only those are initialised). 5) Scan: the same word-skip over group_is_set. 6) plan_aggregate.cpp CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (:230): keep the PerfectHtThresholdSetting check, but also accept when total bits <= 18 and 2^bits * an estimated row width stays below about 8MB per thread. Use a file-local constexpr. Do NOT change the setting's default. Build in the background, check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that q13's inner aggregate becomes PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY, then run the full bench and look closely at q17, q14 and q18.
expected_gain: q13 about -20% (measured with a forced SET in E0003). Small gains on other GROUP BYs over dense integer keys with 13-18 bits (E0003 quick bench hinted at q02, q03, q07). Geomean maybe 2-3%.
generality: Any GROUP BY on integer keys with a stats range of 4k-262k values (customer, part, supplier and date keys), which is common in analytics. Lazy init also helps existing <=12-bit perfect aggregates on tiny inputs. Could get slower: aggregates with a wide stats range but very sparse actual groups and large inputs (random access over a table up to 8MB instead of a compact HT), and plans with many tiny overestimated aggregates (each pays a 262KB memset per thread).
risk: Medium. Correctness: every state must be initialised before Update, Combine or Finalize, and Destroy must skip uninitialised slots (aggregates with destructors, e.g. list or string min/max). The header change rebuilds a moderate number of files. The 18-bit cap must hold, because 23 bits was measured 10x slower.

title: Per-key bloom filter pushdown for multi-key hash joins
hypothesis: In q09 (the slowest template, 114ms) the 2-key join partsupp ⋈ (filtered part/lineitem build side, ~324k rows) probes all 800k partsupp rows. Its probe costs ~0.14-0.16s CPU, and the scan only gets min/max dynamic filters, because JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:775) requires ht->conditions.size()==1. The only reason is that the HT bloom filter is filled with the combined hash of all keys (JoinHashTable::Finalize join_hashtable.cpp:790 loads the stored row hash, and InsertHashes :721 inserts it into bloom_filter). BFTableFilter::Filter (bloom_filter.cpp:90-92) probes with VectorOperations::Hash of the single filter column. A BF on one key column needs that column hashed on its own. ps_partkey alone is very selective here, since p_name LIKE '%ghost%' keeps ~5% of parts. A partkey BF would drop ~95% of partsupp rows in the scan before the probe and the hash computation. The SelectivityOptionalFilter wrapper (BF_THRESHOLD/BF_CHECK_N) already switches off a BF on an unselective key such as ps_suppkey, so pushing a filter on every equality key is safe.
plan: 1) join_hashtable.hpp/.cpp: keep the existing single-key bloom_filter path as it is. Add per-key bloom filters for multi-key equality joins, e.g. `vector<unique_ptr<BloomFilter>> key_bloom_filters` indexed by condition index, plus setter/getter. In AllocatePointerTable (:741), Initialize each requested one with Count(). In Finalize (:775), for each requested key: Gather that key column from row_locations into a Vector (data_collection->Gather with an incremental sel, as at :968/:1487). First verify which layout column holds condition i; equality keys may be reordered (see equality_predicate_columns). Then VectorOperations::Hash it into a hash vector and call key_bf.InsertHashes(hash_vec, count). Only do this work when a key BF was requested. 2) physical_hash_join.cpp: in CanUseBloomFilter, allow conditions.size()>1 when cmp == COMPARE_EQUAL (keep the build_side_has_filter and probe-larger checks). In FinalizeFilters (:899), for multi-key joins, record the condition index join_condition[filter_idx] in the deferred entry and request the key BF for that condition. In PushBloomFilter (:787), for multi-key joins, use that condition's BF, NullValuesAreEqual(cond_idx), conditions[cond_idx].right->ToString() and left->return_type instead of index 0. The deferred vector's pair type may need a third field (a struct or tuple), so update the declarations at physical_hash_join.cpp:212 and join_filter_pushdown.hpp:86. 3) Before the full bench, check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of q09 that the partsupp scan shows an 'IN BF' dynamic filter on ps_partkey, and that its row count falls from 800k to under 100k. Build in the background, since join_hashtable.hpp is included by the join operators.
expected_gain: q09: 10-20% (partsupp probe ~0.15s CPU plus scan and hash work on 800k rows). Small gains are possible on other multi-key equality joins where the build side is filtered. Geomean maybe -1.5% to -3%.
generality: Any equi-join on a composite key (partsupp/lineitem-style composite keys, multi-column fact-to-dimension joins, decorrelated subqueries correlated on 2+ columns) where the build side is filtered. Possible slowdowns: multi-key joins with large unselective build sides pay an extra gather, hash and BF insert per key on the build. The check that the probe is larger than the build, and SelectivityOptionalFilter on the probe side, limit this.
risk: Medium. Correctness depends on mapping each condition index to its layout column and on matching hash semantics. The BF must hash exactly like VectorOperations::Hash on the probe column type; skip keys whose probe column has a cast (has_cast is already checked). NULL handling must use the per-condition NullValuesAreEqual. A header change means a longer rebuild.

title: Collapse adjacent duplicate group keys before hash-table probe in aggregation
hypothesis: q18 (87ms, 3rd slowest) is dominated by the subquery `SELECT l_orderkey FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>312`. Measured with dbe-tool sql: that aggregate takes ~65-72ms hot. A plain sum(l_quantity) scan of lineitem takes 3ms, so nearly all of the time is in GroupedAggregateHashTable (6M rows, 1.5M groups). lineitem is stored clustered by l_orderkey (about 4 consecutive rows per key), so roughly 75% of input rows have the same group key as the row before them. Today each of those rows still pays the full FindOrCreateGroupsInternal path (aggregate_hashtable.cpp:641-814): offset/salt computation, the inner probe loop with a random cache-missing access into `entries`, and a RowMatcher compare against the materialized group row. If equal adjacent keys are detected with a cheap sequential compare of the input vector, only the run heads need to be probed, and the other rows copy the head's address. Clustered or sorted keys are common: order ids, time-series ingestion order, and join outputs that keep probe-side order (for example GROUP BY l_orderkey after a join probed by lineitem in q03-style queries).
plan: In src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp, GroupedAggregateHashTable::FindOrCreateGroupsInternal, after the hashes and addresses vectors are flattened and before the probe loop (i.e. not in the skip_lookups branch), add a file-local static helper that builds a selection of run heads. Row r is a duplicate of r-1 when hashes[r]==hashes[r-1] and every group column is equal at r and r-1, checked with the UnifiedVectorFormat already produced by TupleDataCollection::ToUnifiedFormat (state.partitioned_append_state.chunk_state.vector_data): null-ness must match, and both values are equal or both NULL. Restrict this to group columns of fixed-size physical types (numerics, dates, hugeint) plus string_t compared via Equals; otherwise skip the fast path. If the number of duplicates is 0 (or below about chunk_size/8), use the existing path unchanged. Otherwise run the existing loop with `sel_vector` pointing at a heads SelectionVector and `remaining_entries = head_count` (the inner loop already has a sel_vector->IsSet() template variant, and new_groups_out/empty_vector indices are original row indices, so appends are unaffected). After the loop, fill addresses[r] = addresses[r-1] for each duplicate r in ascending order. Make it adaptive with a member or AggregateHTAppendState counter: after ~16 chunks with less than 1/8 duplicates, disable the check for that hash table, so unclustered inputs pay only a short trial cost. If a new member is needed, put it in AggregateHTAppendState or the GroupedAggregateHashTable header (src/include/duckdb/execution/aggregate_hashtable.hpp) and accept the rebuild; build in the background. UpdateAggregates already handles repeated addresses, as today's path produces them for in-chunk duplicates. Verify q18 with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and check that the results are identical. Also run a GROUP BY with NULL keys and with a multi-column key (l_orderkey, l_linenumber) for correctness.
expected_gain: q18 -15 to -25% (the subquery aggregate is ~70% of its time; probe+compare work drops for ~75% of rows). Small gains are possible on q03, q04 and q18's outer aggregates and on any GROUP BY over join output that keeps lineitem/orders order. Roughly -1.5 to -3% visible geomean.
generality: Any hash aggregate (and DISTINCT, which shares FindOrCreateGroups) whose input has runs of equal keys: sorted or clustered tables, data loaded in time order, joins that keep probe order, and low-cardinality keys in sorted data. Queries on randomly ordered keys pay one sequential compare per row for the first ~16 chunks, after which the check is disabled. That cost is negligible, but tiny aggregates with a high chunk count over random data could see under 1% overhead.
risk: Medium-low. The logic is local to one function and correctness is easy to test (results must match exactly). The main risks are NULL handling in the adjacency compare and interaction with the unpartitioned_data path that uses empty_vector indices. Both are covered by keeping original row indices. Performance risk is small because of the adaptive disable.
